clue.text: Any PC tosh churned out by a brown-noser

indicators.note: something churned out is stirred and turned over, so these nine letters are mixed into a new order

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A grovelling flatterer produces a stream of politically correct rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'churned out' looks like the flatterer's output, but it tells you to rearrange ANY PC TOSH. 'Brown-noser' is crude slang for a crawler.
explanation.definitionFit: A sycophant is a flatterer who fawns on the powerful, exactly what the vulgar slang describes.

clue.text: Genesis joins Thatcher for a spot

parts.note: genesis is an origin or beginning, a birth
Mark Thatcher, the Prime Minister's son, a regular Private Eye target

explanation.surface: The Book of Genesis teams up with a Thatcher to make a place or a blemish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thatcher' points at Margaret, but the piece needed is her son Mark Thatcher, often mocked in Private Eye.
explanation.definitionFit: A birthmark is a coloured patch of skin present from birth, a kind of spot.

clue.text: Time to get kids something to blow their noses on

definitions.text: something to blow their noses on

parts.note: a person's kids are their issue, their offspring

explanation.surface: A parent declares it is the moment to give the children something for their runny noses.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper tissue is the disposable handkerchief people use to wipe a running nose.

clue.text: To back celebrity arse-licking publication is a tragedy

indicators.note: read back, so the little word to runs from right to left

parts.note: Hello! is the glossy magazine of fawning celebrity interviews

explanation.surface: Supporting a fawning celebrity magazine is presented as a disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' looks like 'support', but it reverses 'To' into OT. Hello! is a British celebrity magazine known for flattering coverage.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello is one of Shakespeare's great tragedies, about the jealous Moor of Venice.

clue.text: Taki's was pisspoor sign of fascism

indicators.note: something piss-poor is badly done, so the letters are a botched arrangement to be put right

parts.note: the fodder, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A jab at Taki, the right-wing Spectator columnist, whose sign of fascism was feeble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pisspoor' reads as a verdict on Taki but signals rearranging TAKIS WAS. Taki Theodoracopulos was a Spectator columnist often accused of far-right sympathies.
explanation.definitionFit: The hooked cross was the emblem of the Nazi party and remains the best-known symbol of fascism.

clue.text: One who votes for another unworthy — Labour finally gets in

indicators.note: one letter gets in, entering the middle of the other word

parts.note: poxy is British slang for worthless or rubbishy

indicators.note: finally picks only the closing letter of Labour

parts.note: the word whose last letter is taken

explanation.surface: A political grumble: the unworthy deputy voter, and Labour wins in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' takes the R ending Labour, and 'gets in' puts it inside POXY, informal British for trashy or second-rate.
explanation.definitionFit: A proxy is a person authorised to cast a vote on someone else's behalf.

clue.text: One out to create a good public image, David Steel?

definitions.text: One out to create a good public image
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a public-relations man, whose job is image
second meaning: the Liberal leader campaigned for proportional representation, so he is a man for PR

explanation.walkthrough: PR stands both for public relations and for proportional representation, the Liberal cause David Steel championed; the question mark flags the second, punning sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A publicist works on image, and an advocate of the voting reform is a supporter of the other PR.

clue.text: Having it off with Cyril's the role of Rice, arguably

indicators.note: with it off, the letters have gone off, spoiled and jumbled into another order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Smutty innuendo: having sex with Cyril is supposedly the part Rice plays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having it off' is British slang for sex; read cryptically, 'it' joins CYRILS and 'off' scrambles them. Tim Rice wrote the words for Lloyd Webber musicals; 'arguably' teases whether that counts as poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: Tim Rice wrote the songs' words, so his job in the partnership was that of a songwriter of lyrics.

clue.text: Hear Bron howl for weekly Army issue

indicators.note: hear says the name is taken by its sound, which matches a different spelling

parts.note: Auberon Waugh, known as Bron, the Private Eye diarist
a howl is a cry

explanation.surface: Listen to Auberon Waugh complain about the weekly army newsletter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hear' works on the name: in a British accent WAUGH is said like WAR. Auberon Waugh, nicknamed Bron, wrote a long-running diary column in Private Eye.
explanation.definitionFit: The War Cry is the newspaper the Salvation Army publishes every week.

clue.text: Last-minute withdrawal in order to avoid issue

definitions.text: Last-minute withdrawal in order to avoid issue

parts.words: Last-minute withdrawal in order to avoid issue
parts.note: reads like a politician pulling out late to dodge a contentious question, but issue means children and withdrawal is the contraceptive method

explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' looks like a subject of debate; here it means offspring, as in 3 Down.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin term names the contraceptive practice of pulling out before ejaculation, so pregnancy is avoided.

clue.text: Tebbit type has ruined 'names' going around screwing

indicators.note: the jumbled word goes around the other piece, enclosing it
ruined names are wrecked, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written
screwing is slang for sex

explanation.surface: A Norman Tebbit sort who has wrecked reputations by sleeping around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' rearranges the quoted word into ESMAN, and 'going around' wraps that about the slang for screwing. Essex Man was the 1980s label for the working-class Thatcher voter; Tebbit's Chingford seat was in Essex.
explanation.definitionFit: The journalistic stereotype of the brash right-wing voter from the London fringe matches Tebbit's blunt populist style.

clue.text: Boudoir left Ian knackered — he appeased in vain

parts.note: a boudoir is a lady's private room, a chamber

indicators.note: knackered is British slang for broken or worn out, so these three letters are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: Ian, exhausted, has left the bedroom; the appeaser failed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knackered' turns IAN into AIN. Neville Chamberlain tried to appease Hitler at Munich in 1938.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1930s Prime Minister is remembered for the policy of concessions to Hitler that failed to prevent war.

clue.text: Patsy gives head to old-fashioned silly person, but needs direction first

indicators.note: first places the compass letter at the front of the answer

parts.note: S for south, a compass direction
a head is a headland, a cape
a goat, as in silly old goat, is a dated word for a fool

explanation.surface: A dupe defers to an old fool but must be pointed the right way beforehand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needs direction first' puts S at the front; 'head' means a headland jutting into the sea, not a top.
explanation.definitionFit: A patsy is someone set up to take the blame, which is what a scapegoat is.

clue.text: Strange but true: Tory leader on Ecstasy, as he might have said to a treacherous colleague

definitions.text: as he might have said to a treacherous colleague

indicators.note: in a down answer, one piece on another sits above it
strange letters are odd and unfamiliar, so these are put in a new order

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter, so only the first of Tory is used

parts.note: the word whose first letter is taken
E is the street abbreviation for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Odd but genuine: the Conservative leader on drugs, addressing a backstabber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' rearranges BUT TRUE into ETTUBRU, 'leader' takes T from Tory, and in a down clue 'on' sets T above E. The 'he' is Caesar addressing Brutus, as Thatcher might have to Heseltine in 1990.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesar's reproach to Brutus, his friend among the assassins, is the classic line for betrayal by an ally.

clue.text: Get someone out of office by removing dress?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to expel a priest from holy orders

explanation.walkthrough: 'Office' sounds like a political job; it is the priesthood, and the question mark flags the jokey literal reading of the second half.
explanation.definitionFit: To defrock a priest is to expel him from the ministry, symbolically stripping the clerical gown.

clue.text: Shameful vice once to get pregnant?

indicators.note: a shameful pair of words is disgraced and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A disgraceful former vice leads to a pregnancy.
explanation.definitionFit: To conceive is to become pregnant, the moment a child is started.

clue.text: Greedy heads of privatised industries owning a corporation, grabbing the whole show?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the overpaid bosses of the newly sold-off utilities

definitions.text: owning a corporation, grabbing the whole show?
definitions.meaning: second meaning, playful: corporation is old slang for a paunch, so the owner is plump, and greedy pets grab everything

explanation.walkthrough: Corporation reads as a company, but it is also dated slang for a big belly, which makes its owner fat; the question mark marks the jokey second description.
explanation.definitionFit: The scornful idiom for wealthy, overpaid executives was used constantly of 1990s privatised utility chiefs.

clue.text: Old town which would make an appropriate Without Walls subject?

definitions.text: Old town which would make an appropriate Without Walls subject?

parts.words: Old town which would make an appropriate Without Walls subject?
parts.note: Without Walls was a Channel 4 arts series, and the biblical city famously lost its walls

explanation.walkthrough: Without Walls was a 1990s Channel 4 arts documentary series. In the Book of Joshua the walls of this ancient city fell at the trumpets' blast.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical city is one of the oldest towns on earth, and its walls tumbled down.

clue.text: See 10
Tony, ditching centre, pursues Right with desperate air of curiosity

indicators.note: pursues puts the trimmed name after the rest
desperate letters are wild and frantic, so they are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

indicators.note: ditching the centre leaves only the first and last letters

parts.note: the name whose middle letters are dropped

explanation.surface: Tony Blair, dropping the centre ground, chases the Right with a frantic inquisitive look.
explanation.walkthrough: Blair's critics said he dumped Labour's centre to court the Right; here 'ditching centre' trims the name to TY, 'desperate' makes ARI, and 'pursues' sets TY last.
explanation.definitionFit: A curiosity is an odd or uncommon object, so a rarity in the sense of a collectable oddity.

clue.text: Some Vietnamese who suffered heavy losses

indicators.note: only some of the word is used: a run of its letters

parts.note: the word holds the run of letters inside it, between VIET and the final E

explanation.surface: Some of the Vietnamese people endured terrible casualties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' means part of 'Vietnamese'. The surface suggests the Vietnam War; the definition is the Lloyd's of London investors, called Names, ruined by insurance losses around 1990.
explanation.definitionFit: Lloyd's underwriting members, known by this term, were bankrupted by huge insurance claims in the early 1990s.

clue.text: Thatcher swore it wasn't her intention to stick trade union leaders in the jug!

definitions.text: Thatcher swore it wasn't her intention

indicators.note: to stick one thing in another puts it inside
with to stick, places the union initials within the vessel

parts.note: an urn is a jug-like vessel

indicators.note: leaders are the first letters of the two words

parts.note: the words whose first letters are taken

explanation.surface: Thatcher denied any wish to jail union bosses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaders' gives TU, and 'to stick ... in' puts TU inside the vessel; 'the jug' looks like prison slang but is a container. Thatcher's 1980 line was 'The lady's not for turning.'
explanation.definitionFit: Thatcher vowed never to reverse her policy, a political about-face in the idiom.

clue.text: It takes one real git to make a South American invader

indicators.note: the letters are used to make something new, so they are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written
I, the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Only a true idiot would become a South American aggressor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to make' says I and REAL GIT are rearranged. General Galtieri led the Argentine junta that invaded the Falklands in 1982.
explanation.definitionFit: The Argentine dictator ordered the 1982 Falklands invasion, the South American leader who attacked British territory.

clue.text: Shags date abandoned by Gang of Four member

indicators.note: the date is abandoned, dropped from the surname

parts.note: Bill Rodgers, one of the four Labour figures who founded the SDP

explanation.surface: A sex scandal: a Gang of Four politician stands up a date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abandoned by' drops D from the surname. The Gang of Four were Jenkins, Owen, Williams and Rodgers, who left Labour in 1981. To roger is British slang for having sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are coarse British slang verbs for having sex with someone, so they swap in the third person.

clue.text: Branagh made it with Fonda — very briefly!

parts.note: Henry Fonda, the Hollywood actor, goes with the surname
V is the short form of very

explanation.surface: Innuendo that Branagh slept with a Fonda, though only quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made it with' suggests sex; read cryptically, it is Branagh's 1989 film of Shakespeare's play, and the first name goes with Fonda.
explanation.definitionFit: Kenneth Branagh directed and starred in the 1989 film of Shakespeare's Agincourt history play.

clue.text: Sixties garb causing lustful heavy breathing?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: very short shorts, a fashion of the era
second meaning: panting that is hot, read as two words

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits the garment's name into hot (aroused) and pants (gasps).
explanation.definitionFit: The skimpy shorts were a youth fashion, and aroused gasping is literally heated panting.
